title: Block close: the prayer book
hook: psalms for every mood, and wisdom that knows life is short and good

segments.voice: Yesterday, the books between, the deuterocanon, and your line was in the hand of god. Who did you picture held there? Day four hundred sixty-one.

Fifty days ago we opened this part of the Bible with a tree planted by the water. Since then: a psalm for the night sky and a psalm for the dark night. A cry of my God, my God, why. A deer panting for water. A clean heart, asked for after a terrible failure. Help from the hills. Out of the depths. By the rivers of Babylon. Let everything that has breath. Then Job, a good man who lost everything, and the friends who were wise for seven days and then started talking. Proverbs and its ant. The Preacher and his breath. Love as strong as death. A morning mercy in a ruined city. Today we close the block, and look at what all of it was.
screen: `FIFTY DAYS SINCE THE TREE.` → `PSALMS, JOB, PROVERBS.` → `THE PREACHER AND THE SONG.` → `WHAT WAS ALL OF IT?`

segments.voice: Start with the Psalms. For many centuries they have been the prayer book of Jews and of Christians: monks chant all hundred and fifty in a cycle, churches sing them on Sunday, people whisper them in hospital beds. And the surprise, every time, is how much of it isn't polite. There is joy, in the King James words: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." There is trust: the Lord is my shepherd. But there is also rage, and confusion, and how long, O Lord, and one psalm, the eighty-eighth, that ends in darkness with no answer at all. A large share of the psalms are laments. The Bible's prayer book teaches you to bring the real feeling, not the tidy one. The early church writer Athanasius wrote that in the rest of scripture we read about others, but in the Psalms we find our own words, as if they were written for us. Then the wisdom books, and they keep the same honesty. Job won't accept a cheap answer for suffering, and God, in the end, says Job spoke rightly and his explainers did not. Proverbs says ordinary life, the tongue, the work, the ant, is where wisdom happens. The Preacher says life is breath, and therefore to eat your bread with joy. The Song says love is as strong as death. Lamentations says the mercies are new every morning, even in the ruins. Put all of that together and you get one idea these books share: that everything a human being feels can be brought before God. Christians across the churches pray this way, and the Gospels show Jesus praying a psalm on the cross. Read like this, the prayer book isn't there to make anyone sound holy. It's there to make them honest.
screen: `THE PRAYER BOOK OF TWO FAITHS.` · `NOT POLITE: RAGE, GRIEF, PRAISE.` · `THE PSALMS SPEAK FOR US.` · `WISDOM KEEPS THE SAME HONESTY.` · then, large: `PRAY WHAT YOU FEEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one psalm to keep all year. Settle, and breathe. Let some of them pass by in your mind: the tree by the water, the Lord is my shepherd, as the deer, be still, shamar, De profundis, curiously wrought. Notice which one your heart leans toward. Not the one you think you should choose. The one that sounds like you. When it comes, keep it. That's your psalm for the year, for good days and bad. If you pray, you can pray its first line now. The bell holds the time.
Lament. The honest cry that fills much of the Psalms, closing fifty days of psalms and wisdom: a prayer book for every mood, and wisdom that knows life is short, and good.

Your line: pray what you feel. Today, write your psalm's number somewhere you'll see it, and the next time a strong feeling comes, good or hard, bring it to God or to the page exactly as it is. Day four hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Christians pray the Psalms daily in many forms: monastic communities and the Liturgy of the Hours cycle through them, Orthodox services read the whole Psalter each week, Anglicans pray them through each month, and many Protestants read one a day.

fork.setup: you're furious, or grieving, and you want to pray, but your feelings don't sound holy. what do the Psalms do?
options: wait until you feel calm, then pray.
bring the real feeling, rage and grief included.
pray only praise and keep the rest to yourself.
fork.reveal: the Bible's prayer book is full of how long, O Lord and why. the psalms teach prayer that is honest before it is polite.

original.note: Hebrew name of the book of Psalms: praises, though many of them are laments.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Psalms are gentle, holy-sounding prayers.
what it means: a prayer book for every mood, joy, rage and grief included, with wisdom books that keep the same honesty.
what a scholar hears: the Hebrew title is Tehillim, praises, yet laments are the largest single type. Athanasius wrote that the Psalms speak for us, not only to us.
